Compromised @joyfill 2773 prerelease install or trojanized dist bundle hash on disk AIDelivery Medium
Hunts installation of the hijacked @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts 2773 beta versions and the presence of their trojanized dist bundles by known SHA256. These prereleases carry an obfuscated RAT that runs on import (not install), so catching the package/version, the malicious dist filenames, or the hashes on any developer or CI host is the earliest article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact hijacked package names + the '2773' beta token, the two published SHA256 bundle hashes, and the malicious dist filenames (index.es.js/index.cjs.js/joyfill.min.js for layouts; index.js/index.esm.js/joyfill.min.js for components) from the StepSecurity IOC list — all deterministic IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/malicious-npm-packages-deliver-nodecordrat • https://daily.dev/posts/two-joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised-to-deliver-dev-pop--fexj4roho
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately auditing or uninstalling the compromised version (command line still references joyfill+2773 — check intent)
  • SBOM/SCA scanner echoing the package name+version in its own command line
  • A private mirror re-tagging an unrelated internal '2773' build number for a different fork
  • Security researcher reproducing the IOC in a sandbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which 2773 version installed and whether the host is a developer workstation (the real target) vs a CI runner; check for a follow-on node -e child and outbound to the C2 IPs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the package, pin to a pre-2026-07-28 release (joyfill layouts 0.1.1 / components 4.0.0-rc24 non-2773), and force-rotate all credentials present on the machine (browser, npm, GitHub/gh, SSH, cloud). 3) Hunt: sweep all repos, lockfiles and CI images for any joyfill 2773 string and the two SHA256s; pivot to the persistence and C2 UCs for the same host.

),

     or (FolderPath has @"\node_modules\@joyfill\" and FileName in~ ("index.es.js","index.cjs.js","joyfill.min.js","index.esm.js","index.js"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, User = InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source = "FileWrite"

| order by Timestamp desc

Node.js spawning detached 'node -e' child or Python stealer at import time AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's execution stage: a node process spawning a detached 'node -e' child (the second-stage /$/boot fetcher) or launching a Python interpreter (the staged credential stealer) during a build, test, or import step. Because the payload is import-time, npm install --ignore-scripts does not prevent it. Rationale: The article states the loader 'spawns a detached node -e child that requests /$/boot' and 'stages a Python infostealer' — so a node parent producing a node -e inline-eval child or a python child is the article-specific execution shape, distinct from the install/hash IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/malicious-npm-packages-deliver-nodecordrat
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006 T1204
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling (node-gyp, webpack, playwright) legitimately spawning Python for native module builds
  • Monorepo npm scripts using 'node -e' one-liners
  • Electron dev workflows launching python for asset pipelines
  • node-based test runners shelling out to python coverage tools
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentCmd has_any ("node-gyp","webpack","playwright","jest","electron-builder") or ChildCmd has_any ("node-gyp","coverage","pip ","setup.py"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the node -e child command line and the python invocation — legitimate build children reference package/build paths; malicious ones fetch /$/boot or read browser stores. Correlate with the joyfill 2773 install on the same host. 2) Contain: if the child beacons to a C2 IP or reads browser profiles, isolate the host and kill the node/python tree. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the child PID to the C2 IPs and check for dev-tool persistence patching.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where (FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e")
    or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where (TargetProcessName has "node" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-e")
    or TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3","pythonw.exe","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node/Python beacon to joyfill RAT C2 IPs and distinctive /$/boot request paths AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on a node or python process contacting the four named C2 hosts (166.88.134.62, 23.27.13.43, 198.105.127.210, 23.27.202.27) or the distinctive HTTP request paths the RAT uses (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv). 23.27.13.43 specifically serves the /$/boot second stage. Rationale: Uses the four hardcoded C2 IPs and the distinctive /$/boot, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /u/e, /u/f, /snv request paths from the StepSecurity IOC block; the C2 IPs are deterministic and 23.27.13.43 is documented as serving the /$/boot second stage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/malicious-npm-packages-deliver-nodecordrat
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different tenant re-using one of the C2 IPs after takedown and IP reassignment
  • Threat-intel/EDR product resolving the IOC IPs for enrichment
  • A benign app coincidentally using a /verify-human/ path on an unrelated host (the C2-IP branch remains high-fidelity)
  • Internal red-team replay of the IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node/python and the destination is one of the four C2 IPs (high fidelity); pull the process tree to link back to a joyfill 2773 import. 2) Contain: block the four C2 IPs at egress, isolate the host, and capture node/python memory before killing. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs org-wide for the /$/boot, /0x/js and /verify-human/ paths and enumerate every host that reached the C2 IPs from a node/python process.

Node.js resolving C2 via Tron/Aptos/BSC blockchain dead-drop RPC endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the campaign's signature blockchain dead-drop C2 resolution: a node process querying public Tron (api.trongrid.io), Aptos (fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com) and BNB Smart Chain (bsc-dataseed.binance.org, bsc-rpc.publicnode.com) RPC endpoints to read a transaction whose XOR-decrypted input yields the live C2 address. Node.js reaching blockchain RPCs is anomalous in most enterprises. Rationale: The article and corroborating write-ups describe the loader reading a Tron transaction, following it to a BNB Smart Chain transaction via eth_getTransactionByHash, then XOR-decrypting the input as JavaScript — the pre-extracted blockchain endpoints (trongrid/aptos/bsc) are the dead-drop lookup path. Scoping to node.exe removes benign web3 developer noise on the Defender/Falcon branches. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/blockchain developer tooling or dApps calling api.trongrid.io or bsc-dataseed.binance.org from node
  • A crypto-price or wallet npm dependency polling BSC RPC
  • Hardhat/Foundry test suites hitting public RPC seed nodes
  • Sentinel DNS branch has no process context so any host resolving these domains matches — pair with the node-scoped endpoint branches
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("hardhat","foundry","ethers","web3","truffle")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node.exe and the host is not a blockchain-dev workstation; correlate with a joyfill 2773 import and any subsequent connection to the four C2 IPs. 2) Contain: if correlated, isolate the host and block the C2 IPs; blocking the public RPC endpoints is generally not viable, so pivot on the process context. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host where node.exe resolved these RPC endpoints and cross-reference against the package-install UC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsQueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Endpoint DNS Query to Tron/Aptos/BSC RPC Dead-Drop Endpoints (joyfill RAT)
id: 8e5b2a17-0d94-4c6a-b31f-6a2c9f74d0e1
description: Detects DNS resolution of the public Tron/Aptos/BNB Smart Chain RPC endpoints used by the joyfill npm RAT to resolve its rotating C2 via a blockchain dead drop.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:

logsource:

detection:

      - 'fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com'
      - 'bsc-dataseed.binance.org'
      - 'bsc-rpc.publicnode.com'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) @DestinationHostname:(api.trongrid.io OR fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com OR bsc-dataseed.binance.org OR bsc-rpc.publicnode.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest (DomainName=/trongrid\.io$/i OR DomainName=/aptoslabs\.com$/i OR DomainName=/bsc-dataseed\.binance\.org$/i OR DomainName=/publicnode\.com$/i) | ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Persistence: node.exe patching @vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js or global npm CLI AIInstallation High
Hunts the trojan's persistence: a node process modifying trusted developer-tool files that run routinely — the @vscode/deviceid module (VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity), the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI — to insert a self-reloading block. Legitimate updates to these files come from their own installers, not from node.exe. Rationale: Directly maps the article's named persistence targets (@vscode/deviceid used by VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity, the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI) with node.exe as the modifying process — a Node runtime rewriting these editor/IM files is abnormal outside an installer, making the process+path pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/malicious-npm-packages-deliver-nodecordrat
ATT&CKT1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VS Code / Cursor auto-update rewriting @vscode/deviceid via its own updater (not node.exe — verify initiating process)
  • A legitimate 'npm install -g' rewriting the global npm CLI directory during a Node upgrade
  • Discord's own client updater refreshing its core module
  • A developer manually patching main.js of a locally-built GitHub Desktop fork
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "update"
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify node.exe (not the app's own updater/installer) modified the file, and diff the modified module against a known-good copy for an injected self-reload block. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the patched files from a clean install, and rotate credentials. 3) Hunt: check the same host for the joyfill 2773 import, the node -e / python execution, and C2 beacons; sweep other developer machines for the identical file modifications by node.exe.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\@vscode\deviceid"
    or FolderPath has "discord_desktop_core"
    or (FolderPath has "GitHub Desktop" and FileName =~ "main.js")
    or FolderPath has @"\npm\node_modules\npm\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\@vscode\deviceid"
    or TargetFilePath has "discord_desktop_core"
    or (TargetFilePath has "GitHub Desktop" and TargetFileName =~ "main.js")
    or TargetFilePath has @"\npm\node_modules\npm\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["git-tanstack.com", "check.git-service.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48027", "CVE-2026-45321")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse (< 2.0.2, CVE-2026-54658) in software inventory AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts/containers running @hypequery/clickhouse below the patched 2.0.2 release that carries the escapeValue() SQL-injection flaw (CVE-2026-54658). This is exposure hunting for the specific vulnerable npm package named in the advisory, not a behavioural attack detection. Rationale: Direct match on the CVE id from the advisory (CVE-2026-54658) plus the affected package @hypequery/clickhouse < 2.0.2; MDVM/CIM Vulnerabilities inventory is the cleanest place to enumerate exposed assets before exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present in a dev/test container that is not internet-exposed and takes no user-controlled parameters
  • App wraps hypequery only with server-generated (non-user) parameter values, so the flaw is not reachable
  • Vendored copy pinned at 2.0.2+ but TVM fingerprint lags and still shows old metadata
  • Internal tooling image flagged but decommissioned / not running
  • Package inventoried as a transitive dependency that is never invoked at runtime
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is truly < 2.0.2 and whether the host serves user-controlled ClickHouse queries (internet-facing API vs internal batch job). 2) Contain: prioritise upgrade to @hypequery/clickhouse 2.0.2 on any asset that passes untrusted input as query parameters; where patching lags, front the endpoint with a WAF rule blocking backslash-terminated parameter values. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 to check whether the exposed asset has already received backslash-quote injection payloads in web or ClickHouse query logs.

ClickHouse SQLi via trailing backslash quote-escape in web/API parameters (CVE-2026-54658) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests whose parameter values carry the CVE-2026-54658 exploitation signature — a backslash immediately before a single quote (raw \' or URL-encoded %5c%27) used to break out of the escapeValue() string literal — combined with SQL syntax tokens. Targets the actual exploitation attempt against apps using @hypequery/clickhouse. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2026-54658 breakout mechanic from the advisory (trailing backslash escaping the closing single quote in escapeValue()) rendered as raw \' and URL-encoded %5c%27, gated by SQL tokens so it is specific to injection rather than any backslash in a URL. Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows file paths in a legitimate parameter (e.g. ?path=C:\dir\) that happen to precede a quote plus a word like 'select'
  • Security scanners / DAST (Burp, sqlmap, Acunetix) probing the app in an authorized test
  • Rich-text or code-snippet form fields legitimately containing backslashes and SQL keywords
  • Analytics dashboards passing SQL fragments as URL parameters by design
  • WAF-normalised double-encoding producing %255c%2527 that this rule under-matches (tune encoding variants)
Suppression filter
| where not (csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)[a-z]:%5c" and csUserAgent has_any ("sqlmap","nuclei","acunetix","burp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode csUriQuery and confirm a backslash actually terminates a parameter value before a quote followed by injected SQL; check src IP reputation and whether the target app depends on @hypequery/clickhouse. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and add a rule rejecting parameter values ending in backslash to ClickHouse-backed endpoints; if the app is < 2.0.2, expedite the patch. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src/time to UC3 (ClickHouse query log) to confirm whether the injection reached the database, and review responses/status codes for data exfiltration volume.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
// backslash-quote escape (raw or URL-encoded) = the CVE-2026-54658 breakout primitive
| where csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)(%5c%27|%5c'|\\')"
// require SQL syntax alongside the escape to cut generic noise
| where csUriQuery has_any ("union","select","information_schema","sleep(","benchmark(","concat(")
    or csUriQuery contains "--" or csUriQuery contains "/*"
    or csUriQuery matches regex @"(?i)or[%20\s]+\d+=\d+"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs WebDAV --no-delete bypass: DELETE blocked (403) then MOVE succeeds (2xx) on same path AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core CVE-2026-64863 exploit signature on WebDAV/HTTP logs: a client's DELETE to a resource is correctly rejected with 403 by --no-delete, then the same client issues a MOVE for the same source path that returns 201/204, deleting or clobbering the file the policy was meant to protect. Correlating the blocked DELETE with the successful MOVE on the same source+path within a short window isolates deliberate bypass probing from benign WebDAV traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit control-flow: DELETE returns 403 while MOVE on the same source path returns 201 (rename) or 204 (Overwrite:T RemoveAll). Same src+URL pairing of a blocked delete and a successful move is the CVE-2026-64863 fingerprint, not a generic WebDAV template. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606 • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV servers (SharePoint, Nextcloud, IIS WebDAV) where a client legitimately DELETEs then MOVEs unrelated files
  • WebDAV-aware clients (Windows Explorer redirector, Cyberduck, Cadaver) that retry a delete as a move-to-trash operation
  • Backup/sync agents that receive 403 on a locked resource then rename it
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) legitimately probing WebDAV verbs during an authorized scan
  • Web app that returns 403 for DELETE by policy but permits MOVE for renames as intended design
Suppression filter
// Scope to hosts you know run goshs (WebDAV file drop), e.g. filter DstHostname/dest to the artifact-server inventory, and require the DELETE and MOVE to share the SAME SrcIpAddr and Url before alerting.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the destination host is a goshs instance (banner `goshs/vX`) started with `--no-delete`/`-w`; pull the full request pair for src IP + URL and check whether the MOVE 204 carried `Overwrite: T`. 2) CONTAIN: Stop/patch the goshs service (upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is delete-gated) or restrict the WebDAV port to trusted IPs; snapshot the served directory before further loss. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all MOVE 2xx from the same src IP across the served tree, check filesystem delete/rename events by the goshs process, and review other goshs advisories (CVE-2026-50138 read-only/upload-only bypass) on the same host.
let Window = 60s;
let Blocked = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" and HttpStatusCode == "403"
| project BlockTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "MOVE" and HttpStatusCode in ("201","204")
| join kind=inner Blocked on SrcIpAddr, Url, DstHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (BlockTime .. BlockTime + Window)
| project TimeGenerated, BlockTime, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval blocked_delete=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), move_ok=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0)
| stats sum(blocked_delete) as blocked_deletes sum(move_ok) as move_success values(status) as statuses values(http_method) as verbs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src url dest
| where blocked_deletes>0 AND move_success>0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.dest _time span=1s
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval blocked_delete=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status==403,1,0), move_ok=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status==201 OR status==204),1,0)
| stats sum(blocked_delete) as blocked_deletes sum(move_ok) as move_success values(status) as statuses values(http_method) as verbs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src url dest
| where blocked_deletes>0 AND move_success>0
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
goshs process deletes or renames files despite --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 impact) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms real data loss from the WebDAV MOVE bypass by hunting file deletion/rename events whose initiating process is goshs while its command line carries --no-delete. Because --no-delete is supposed to make goshs never remove files, any FileDeleted/FileRenamed originated by that process under that flag is the bypass executing (rename removes the source; Overwrite:T triggers RemoveAll on the destination). Rationale: Pins to two article facts: the initiating binary is `goshs`, and its `--no-delete` command line is what the deletion is supposed to be impossible under — so goshs itself performing FileDeleted/FileRenamed is direct impact confirmation of the MOVE bypass rather than a generic file-deletion query. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/GO-2026-4606
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • goshs run WITHOUT --no-delete where deletion/rename is expected behaviour (filter requires --no-delete so this is largely excluded)
  • Authorized red-team using goshs as a legitimate file-drop and cleaning up its own artifacts
  • Operator manually restarting goshs and clearing the served directory
  • A differently-named binary containing the substring 'goshs' in an unrelated toolchain
  • Antivirus quarantining a file inside the goshs-served path (initiating process would be the AV, not goshs)
Suppression filter
// Already tight: the --no-delete requirement excludes normal goshs deletion. To further reduce noise, restrict FolderPath/TargetFilePath to the goshs served directory (the value passed to `-d`).
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the goshs command line to confirm `--no-delete`/`-w`, and list the deleted/renamed file paths and their prior contents from backups or file-audit history. 2) CONTAIN: Kill the goshs process and upgrade to v2.1.4+ (MOVE now delete-gated); restore any destroyed artifacts from snapshot; restrict the WebDAV port. 3) HUNT: Correlate each deletion timestamp with the WebDAV MOVE 2xx access-log entry (UC1) to identify the source IP, then sweep for the same actor touching other goshs hosts or exploiting sibling goshs CVEs (CVE-2026-50138).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "goshs"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, PreviousFolderPath, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs deployment: WebDAV file-server started with --no-delete (CVE-2026-64863 exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts running a goshs instance launched with the --no-delete protection flag (and WebDAV enabled), which on goshs <= v2.1.3 / <= v1.1.4 is silently bypassable via MOVE. This is a pre-exploitation exposure hunt so defenders can patch to v2.1.4+ or firewall the WebDAV port before the DELETE/MOVE bypass is abused. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact vulnerable invocation (`goshs -w --no-delete -d ...` / `--webdav --no-delete`) and affected versions (<= 2.1.3 / <= 1.1.4). Finds the exploitable configuration itself, giving defenders a patch-before-abuse window rather than waiting for the MOVE to fire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration tests / red-team engagements legitimately standing up goshs for file transfer
  • Security lab / training environments running goshs intentionally
  • Instances already upgraded to v2.1.4+ where the flag combination is present but the bug is patched (validate version from banner)
  • Internal-only goshs on an isolated segment where the WebDAV port is unreachable by untrusted clients
  • A wrapper script or alias named 'goshs' unrelated to the file server
Suppression filter
// Reduce authorized-usage noise by excluding known pentest jump hosts: | where DeviceName !in~ ("redteam-01","pentest-lab-01")  — populate with your sanctioned goshs operator hosts.
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the goshs version (banner `goshs/vX.Y.Z` or package metadata) and whether the WebDAV port is exposed to untrusted networks. 2) CONTAIN: If <= v2.1.3 (or v1 <= 1.1.4), upgrade to v2.1.4+ where MOVE is gated by --no-delete, or firewall the WebDAV listener to trusted IPs only. 3) HUNT: For any exposed vulnerable host, pivot to UC1 (DELETE-403/MOVE-2xx web-log correlation) and UC2 (goshs file deletion) to determine whether the bypass was already exercised, and inventory other goshs hosts org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--webdav","-w")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs launched with vulnerable SFTP empty-credential basic-auth (CVE-2026-62325) AIInstallation High
Hunts endpoint launches of the goshs file-server binary in the specific vulnerable configuration: SFTP mode (-sftp) plus a basic-auth string (-b) whose username or password segment is empty, and no host key file (-fkf). This exact combination leaves both SSH auth handlers nil, causing gliderlabs/ssh to set NoClientAuth=true and expose unauthenticated file read/write/delete/rename. Rationale: Uses the article's exact vulnerable-config primitives: -sftp + -b with an empty username (':pass') or empty password ('admin:') segment and absence of -fkf, the precise combination that leaves PasswordHandler/PublicKeyHandler nil. Cross-checked against the GitLab GLAD advisory (fix v2.1.4, CVSS 9.1, CWE-306) and the CVE-2026-40884 SentinelOne / GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv writeups confirming the -b syntax. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / penetration-test engagement intentionally standing up goshs for file transfer during an assessment.
  • Security researcher reproducing CVE-2026-62325 or CVE-2026-40884 in a lab or CTF box.
  • Sysadmin using goshs as a quick ad-hoc file-drop and terminating the basic-auth string with a trailing colon by mistake.
  • A patched host (v2.1.4+) where the process still runs but the sanity check aborts startup — the process-create event still fires before exit.
  • Unrelated binary or script whose name tokenizes to 'goshs' in a wrapper command line.
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("REDTEAM","PENTEST","-LAB","CTF"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and host — confirm the -b value truly has an empty username/password segment and that -fkf is absent; check goshs version (vuln <= 2.1.3) and whether the SFTP port (PoC default 2121) is listening/internet-facing via DeviceNetworkInfo/netstat. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, kill the goshs process, block the listening port at host firewall, and isolate if the host is internet-exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'goshs unauthenticated SFTP inbound connections' and 'goshs process file read/write/delete' on the same DeviceId to determine whether any remote client already accessed files, and scope other hosts running goshs org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s]+|[^'\s:]+:)('|\s|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+'?(:[^'\s]+|[^'\s:]+:)('|\s|$)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

goshs unauthenticated SFTP listener — remote inbound connections accepted AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces remote clients connecting to a goshs-hosted SFTP/SSH listener, evidencing use of the CVE-2026-62325 unauthenticated access. Because the vulnerable server installs no auth handler, any inbound accept on the goshs process port is a client obtaining file access without credentials. Rationale: Article states unauthenticated SFTP file access is possible remotely; on the host the tell is inbound connections accepted by the goshs process (which listens for SFTP, PoC port 2121). Surfaces LocalPort and remote client IPs so an analyst can confirm external exposure without a hardcoded port. Sentinel left blank: no listed Sentinel table reliably binds an inbound socket accept to the goshs process image in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned use of goshs for internal file distribution where connecting clients are legitimate operators.
  • Vulnerability scanner or internal ASM tool probing the goshs SFTP port.
  • The pentester's own SFTP client during an authorized engagement.
  • Health-check / uptime monitoring hitting the listener port.
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy keepalives to the goshs port.
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each RemoteClient IP, determine internal vs external and whether it maps to a known operator; confirm the LocalPort is the goshs SFTP port and whether it is internet-reachable. 2) Contain: if external or unknown clients are present, kill goshs, block the port, and preserve the process command line to confirm the empty-credential config (link to the process-launch UC on the same host). 3) Hunt: enumerate files touched by the goshs process (file-collection UC) during the connection window to assess read/write/exfil, and check firewall/VPC logs for data volume egress to the client IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "goshs"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), RemoteClients=make_set(RemoteIP, 100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by Connections desc

| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), RemoteClients=make_set(RemoteIP, 100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by Connections desc

goshs process file read/write/delete — collection via unauthenticated SFTP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts filesystem operations performed by the goshs process, the collection/staging evidence of the CVE-2026-62325 bypass being used (article: unauthenticated read, write, delete, rename). goshs is a pentest file-server binary rarely present legitimately, so its file activity on managed endpoints is inherently notable. Rationale: Directly grounded in the article's stated impact ('Unauthenticated SFTP file access (read, write, delete, rename)'). Pivots on the goshs process as the file-operation initiator rather than a path, since the served directory is arbitrary; scoped to the rare goshs binary to keep signal high. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory describing the same read/write impact. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-62325/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/
ATT&CKT1005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal use of goshs to host and serve files where the operator uploads/downloads content.
  • Red-team engagement staging or exfil testing through goshs.
  • goshs writing its own transient/temp or log files during normal operation.
  • Analyst or admin transferring files to a colleague via a short-lived goshs instance.
  • Backup or sync job interacting with a directory goshs also touches (rename/delete churn).
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("REDTEAM","PENTEST","-LAB","CTF"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the FolderPath / TargetFileName set — are sensitive directories (config, keys, docs) being read or written, and does the initiating command line match the vulnerable empty-credential config? 2) Contain: if unauthorized, terminate goshs, quarantine any attacker-written payloads (FileCreated by goshs), and snapshot the served directory for IR. 3) Hunt: correlate to inbound-connection UC to attribute file ops to specific remote client IPs and time windows, then search DeviceNetworkEvents/proxy for outbound transfer of the same filenames to gauge exfiltration.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "goshs"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName

Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for any host that resolved or connected to cubepilot.org or its subdomains (portal, discuss/forum, docs) during the 24 July 2026 DNS-hijack window, when traffic was redirected to attacker infrastructure holding fraudulent TLS certs. Any credentials entered on those services may have been captured. Surfaces the resolved RemoteIP so an analyst can identify the attacker-controlled address. Rationale: Anchors on the exact victim domain (cubepilot.org and subdomains portal/discuss/docs confirmed on CubePilot's own security notice) bounded to the 24 Jul 2026 hijack window; make_set on RemoteIP/DnsResponseName surfaces the attacker-controlled resolution so no attacker IP needs to be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately browsing docs.cubepilot.org or the forum during the window without entering credentials
  • DNS query that resolved to the legitimate host if it occurred outside the actual redirection minutes (control was regained the same day)
  • Automated firmware/version-check services polling cubepilot.org on a schedule
  • CI/CD or package tooling pulling from CubePilot repos
  • Security team already testing/validating the domain post-incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ResolvedIPs for each hit; any answer outside CubePilot's normal hosting ASN during 24 Jul is the attacker endpoint — pivot all hosts sharing that IP. 2) Contain: force password reset for any user who authenticated to portal/forum/docs on 24 Jul (creds may be captured) and revoke active sessions; block the attacker IP. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for the affected users signing in from anomalous IPs post-24 Jul, and check for password reuse alerts across SSO/VPN/email.

| where RemoteUrl has "cubepilot.org"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), ResolvedIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen asc

CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for firmware images or any file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 July 2026 — the window CubePilot flagged as unverified pending checksum review. Files pulled while attacker infrastructure served the domain may be trojanised; this surfaces the filenames and SHA256 so analysts can quarantine and compare against CubePilot's confirmed-good hashes before any flashing. Rationale: Keys on FileOriginUrl containing cubepilot.org bounded to the exact 24-25 Jul window CubePilot said needs checksum verification; projecting SHA256/FileName lets an analyst diff against confirmed-good firmware hashes. Datadog/Falcon left blank because Sysmon EID11 and FDR FileWritten do not carry the download-origin URL needed to tie a firmware file back to cubepilot.org. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firmware download later confirmed clean once CubePilot publishes verified checksums
  • Documentation/PDF or non-firmware asset pulled from cubepilot.org (not a flashable image)
  • Re-download of a pre-24 Jul firmware that a developer already had
  • File served from a CDN/mirror rather than the hijacked origin
  • Automated build agent caching CubePilot artifacts
Suppression filter
| where FileName has_any (".apj",".px4",".bin",".hex",".elf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct SHA256 + FileName from the hits; compare each hash against CubePilot's confirmed-good firmware manifest — any hash not on the allow-list is suspect. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block flashing on affected engineering hosts, and isolate any UAV/bench system that was already flashed from a 24-25 Jul image pending inspection. 3) Hunt: on hosts that downloaded a suspect image, look for the flashing tool executing (ground-station/uploader), unexpected child processes, and outbound connections from the file's downloading process to non-CubePilot IPs.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
